tasks.title: Measure Route SLA Performance
tasks.context: Network leadership wants an offline route-level SLA view using synthetic delivered shipments.
tasks.goal: Count total and on-time shipments at the correct route grain.
tasks.prompt: Query logistics_shipments. Group by route_code and count all rows plus rows where actual_hours <= promised_hours.
hints: The table is already one row per synthetic shipment.
A shipment is on time when actual_hours <= promised_hours.
Use GROUP BY route_code and a conditional SUM or CASE expression.
tasks.explanation: SLA analysis must preserve the route grain and distinguish total volume from on-time volume.

tasks.title: Validate the Shipment Extract
tasks.context: Before a network review, you receive synthetic shipment, route and cost data.
tasks.goal: Apply operational data-quality checks before calculating SLA or cost KPIs.
tasks.prompt: Which checks should be completed before analysis?
expectedSelections: Validate promised_hours, actual_hours, weight_kg and shipping_cost are non-negative.
Standardize route and hub category labels before grouping.
Confirm status definitions before mixing delivered and non-delivered shipments in SLA calculations.
hints: Start with record identity and grain.
Then validate numeric domains.
Categorical consistency and status definitions affect grouping and denominators.
tasks.explanation: Reliable logistics KPIs require valid identifiers, plausible numeric fields, standardized route labels and a documented SLA denominator.
options: Check shipment_id uniqueness.
Validate promised_hours, actual_hours, weight_kg and shipping_cost are non-negative.
Standardize route and hub category labels before grouping.
Confirm status definitions before mixing delivered and non-delivered shipments in SLA calculations.
Delete every late shipment because it is an outlier.
Replace all high costs with the overall mean without investigation.

tasks.title: Interpret a Route SLA Difference
tasks.context: One route has a lower observed on-time percentage than another in a small synthetic sample.
tasks.goal: Avoid overclaiming from small route samples.
tasks.expectedAnswer: Treat the observed SLA gap as a signal, but compare more shipments and control for route distance, weight and operating conditions before claiming the route itself causes delays
hints: Small denominators are noisy.
Route mix can differ in distance, weight or operating conditions.
Association is not automatically causation.
tasks.explanation: A route-level SLA difference is useful for prioritizing investigation, but causal claims require larger and better-controlled evidence.
options: Treat the observed SLA gap as a signal, but compare more shipments and control for route distance, weight and operating conditions before claiming the route itself causes delays
The route code alone definitely causes every delay
Ignore SLA because percentages are never useful
Remove all late shipments before comparing routes

tasks.title: Find Network Throughput Gaps
tasks.context: The network team has a day-of-week shipment forecast and planned processing throughput.
tasks.goal: Identify days where expected demand exceeds planned throughput.
tasks.deliverable: Return day_name and capacity_gap for positive gaps only.
tasks.prompt: Query logistics_throughput_forecast. Return day_name and expected_shipments - planned_throughput AS capacity_gap where expected shipments exceed planned throughput.
hints: Capacity gap = expected demand - planned throughput.
Keep only positive gaps.
The table is already one row per day name.
tasks.explanation: This turns a forecast into an operational capacity signal while preserving uncertainty around the forecast itself.

tasks.title: Find Peak Warehouse Utilization
tasks.context: Warehouse leaders want the highest observed ending-inventory utilization in each synthetic warehouse.
tasks.goal: Convert ending inventory and capacity into a peak utilization percentage.
tasks.deliverable: Return warehouse and peak_utilization_pct rounded to one decimal.
tasks.prompt: Query logistics_inventory_flow. Calculate 100.0 * ending_units / capacity_units for each row, then return the maximum by warehouse rounded to one decimal.
hints: Utilization is ending_units divided by capacity_units.
Multiply by 100.0 to keep decimal division.
Use MAX after calculating row-level utilization.
tasks.explanation: Peak utilization highlights congestion risk but should be paired with duration, throughput and service metrics before changing capacity.

tasks.title: Compare Route Cost per Kilogram
tasks.context: Finance wants a route-level normalized cost metric rather than raw shipping cost alone.
tasks.goal: Calculate shipping cost per kilogram at the route level.
tasks.deliverable: Return route_code and cost_per_kg rounded to one decimal.
tasks.prompt: Query logistics_shipments. Return route_code and ROUND(SUM(shipping_cost) / SUM(weight_kg), 1) AS cost_per_kg grouped by route_code.
hints: Normalize cost by shipment weight.
Aggregate cost and weight before dividing.
Round the route-level ratio to one decimal.
tasks.explanation: Normalized cost supports fairer route comparison than raw cost, but still needs service level and route complexity context.

tasks.title: Design a Fair Route Cohort
tasks.context: A new dispatch process is introduced on one route and leadership asks whether it improved SLA.
tasks.goal: Choose a defensible before/after comparison design.
tasks.prompt: How should the analyst structure the comparison?
tasks.expectedAnswer: Compare the same route across comparable day and shipment-mix periods before and after the process change, while tracking volume, weight and capacity so mix shifts are visible
hints: Keep the route context comparable.
Shipment volume and weight mix can change.
A before/after result is stronger when operating conditions are visible.
tasks.explanation: Operational cohort design should reduce mix differences and surface other changes that could explain SLA movement.
options: Compare the same route across comparable day and shipment-mix periods before and after the process change, while tracking volume, weight and capacity so mix shifts are visible
Compare one route before the change with a different route after the change
Ignore shipment volume because SLA percentage is enough
Remove late shipments before creating the cohorts

tasks.title: Write the Network Executive Message
tasks.context: The synthetic data shows weekend throughput gaps, route-level SLA variation and high warehouse utilization.
tasks.goal: Communicate a bounded, actionable network recommendation.
tasks.expectedAnswer: Weekend forecast demand exceeds planned throughput and some routes show weaker SLA while warehouses approach capacity; validate the pattern over more periods and test routing, staffing and capacity scenarios before rollout
hints: State the observed signals first.
Do not claim one route code causes delay.
Recommend scenario testing before operational rollout.
tasks.explanation: Strong logistics communication connects SLA, capacity and cost signals to controlled operational decisions without overstating causality.
options: Weekend forecast demand exceeds planned throughput and some routes show weaker SLA while warehouses approach capacity; validate the pattern over more periods and test routing, staffing and capacity scenarios before rollout
Close the worst route immediately because the route code causes delays
Ignore warehouse utilization because only delivery time matters
Increase every warehouse and route budget without scenario analysis

tasks.title: Investigate Delay Drivers
tasks.context: NS-1 has the weakest observed SLA in the synthetic sample. Leadership asks what is driving the delays.
tasks.goal: Choose an analysis plan that separates route association from operational drivers.
tasks.prompt: What should the analyst do next?
tasks.expectedAnswer: Compare late versus on-time shipments on weight, day, origin and destination context, then add hub and capacity signals before testing whether the route effect remains
hints: Start with late versus on-time shipments.
Look for differences in shipment mix and operating context.
A route label can proxy for several underlying causes.
tasks.explanation: Delay-driver analysis should move from a route-level signal to measurable operating factors before recommending a network change.
options: Compare late versus on-time shipments on weight, day, origin and destination context, then add hub and capacity signals before testing whether the route effect remains
Assume the route code itself is the root cause
Delete late shipments and recalculate SLA
Use only average shipping cost to explain delay

tasks.title: Forecast Network Throughput
tasks.context: Weekend shipment demand is repeatedly higher than early-week demand and planners need next month's throughput input.
tasks.goal: Choose a defensible first forecasting approach for operations planning.
tasks.prompt: Which approach should the analyst use first?
tasks.expectedAnswer: Model recurring day-of-week seasonality over multiple comparable weeks, back-test forecast error, and provide base, low and high demand scenarios for capacity planning
hints: One busy weekend is not a forecast.
Repeated day-of-week differences are seasonality.
Operations planning benefits from forecast error and scenario ranges.
tasks.explanation: A useful throughput forecast captures repeatable seasonality, is back-tested, and communicates uncertainty through scenarios.
options: Model recurring day-of-week seasonality over multiple comparable weeks, back-test forecast error, and provide base, low and high demand scenarios for capacity planning
Use the single busiest Saturday as every future day's forecast
Assume every day has identical shipment demand
Increase throughput everywhere without measuring forecast error
